richText.plainText: How do you find and exploit them?
Authentication identifies the user and confirms that they are who they say they are.
Windows-integrated authentication using NTLM or Kerberos
Authentication Vulnerabilities arise from insecure implementation of the authentication mechanisms in an application.
Having no or minimal controls over the quality of users' passwords.
Very short or blank passwords allowed
Common dictionary words or names accepted
Password is the same as the username
Level 8 — PASSLESS — Passwordless (WebAuthN, FIDO2) — Vulnerable to: Hardware compromise, Force
Level 7 — CODELESS — App-based Codeless 2FA — Vulnerable to: Malware, Force
Level 6 — APP2FA — App-based 2FA Codes (Authenticator, Authy) — Vulnerable to: Phishing, Malware
Level 5 — SMS2FA — SMS-based 2FA Codes — Vulnerable to: Phishing, SIM-swapping
Level 4 — PASSMAN — Password Manager (1Password, LastPass) — Vulnerable to: Account reset / Takeover
Level 3 — QUALPASS — Quality Passwords (long, random, special chars) — Vulnerable to: Password dumps / Cracking
Level 2 — UNIQPASS — Unique Passwords (too short or simple) — Vulnerable to: Live password guessing
Level 1 — SHARPASS — Shared Passwords (reused across sites) — Vulnerable to: Credential stuffing
Consumer Authentication Strength Maturity Model (CASMM) v6
Application permits brute force or other automated attacks on:
The application outputs a verbose error message that allows for username enumeration
Incorrect username → "Sign in failed. Incorrect username."
Incorrect password → "Sign in failed. Incorrect password."
Different messages reveal whether a username exists in the system, enabling targeted attacks
The application uses an unencrypted HTTP connection to transmit login credentials
HTTP — credentials visible in plaintext in network traffic (Wireshark shows username/password in cleartext)
HTTPS — credentials encrypted in transit, not visible to a network observer
Design weaknesses in the forgotten password functionality usually make the weakest link that can be used to attack the application's overall authentication logic
Example weakness: secret question "What street did you live on in Sierra Vista?" — answers are easily guessable or researched
Insecure implementation of the MFA function
cookie to the victim's username and compromise the victim's account
Bypasses the need to know the victim's verification code
Uses plain text, encrypted, or weakly hashed password data stores
All of the following are insecure — reversible or crackable
Confidentiality — Access to other users' data
Integrity — Access to update other users' data
Availability — Access to delete users and their data
Can sometimes be chained with other vulnerabilities to gain remote code execution on the host operating system
Authentication vulnerabilities moved from A2 in 2013/2017 to A7 (Identification and Authentication Failures) in 2021
A2 – Broken Authentication and Session Management
A7 – Missing Function Level Access Control
A9 – Using Components with Known Vulnerabilities
A9 – Using Components with Known Vulnerabilities
A8 – Software and Data Integrity Failures
A9 – Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
Review the website for any description of the password rules
Password is the same as the username
If self-registration is possible, attempt to register several accounts with different kinds of weak passwords
If you control a single account and password change is possible, attempt to change the password to various weak values
Manually submit several bad login attempts for an account you control
If it works, there is no lockout mechanism
Run a brute force attack to enumerate the valid password
After 10 failed login attempts, if the application does NOT return a message about account lockout, attempt to log in correctly
If the account is locked out, monitor the requests and responses to determine if the lockout mechanism is insecure
NOTE: Apply this test on all authentication pages (Login, OTP, Change password)
Testing Improper Restriction of Authentication Attempts
Submit a request with a valid username and an invalid password
Submit a request with an invalid username
Review both responses for any differences in
If there is a difference, run a brute force attack to enumerate the list of valid usernames in the application
NOTE: Apply this test on all authentication pages
Perform a successful login while monitoring all traffic in both directions between the client and server
Look for instances where credentials are submitted in a URL query string or as a cookie, or transmitted back from the server to the client
Attempt to access the application over HTTP and check if there are any redirections to HTTPS
Identify if the application has any forgotten password functionality
If it does, perform a complete walk-through using an account you control while intercepting the requests/responses in a proxy
Review the functionality to determine if it allows for username enumeration or brute-force attacks
Obtain a number of these URLs and attempt to identify any predictable patterns or sensitive information in the URL
Check if the URL is long lived and does not expire
If the application generates an email containing a recovery URL
Identify if the application uses a multistage login mechanism
If it does, perform a complete walk-through using an account you control while intercepting the requests/responses in a proxy
Review the functionality to determine if it allows for username enumeration or brute-force attacks
Testing Defects in Multistage Login Mechanism
Review all the application's authentication-related functionality
If you find any instances where the user's password is transmitted to the client (plaintext or obfuscated), this indicates insecure storage
If you gain RCE on the server, review the database to determine if the passwords are stored insecurely
Conduct technical interviews with developers to review how passwords are stored in the backend database
How to Find and Exploit Authentication Flaws
Username enumeration via subtly different responses
Broken brute-force protection, multiple credentials per request
Always use an encrypted channel (HTTPS) when sending user credentials
Only POST requests should be used to transmit credentials to the server
Stored credentials must be hashed and salted using cryptographically secure algorithms
Use identical, generic error messages on the login form when the user enters incorrect credentials (prevent username enumeration)
Use a simple password checker to provide real-time feedback on password strength (e.g., zxcvbn JavaScript library)
Implement an effective password policy compliant with NIST 800-63-b guidelines
Implement robust brute force protection on all authentication pages
Audit any verification or validation logic thoroughly to eliminate flaws
2.4.1 — Verify that passwords are stored in a form resistant to offline attacks. Passwords SHALL be salted and hashed using an approved one-way key derivation or password hashing function.
2.4.2 — Verify that the salt is at least 32 bits in length and chosen arbitrarily to minimize salt value collisions. For each credential, a unique salt value and resulting hash SHALL be stored.
2.4.3 — Verify that if PBKDF2 is used, the iteration count SHOULD be as large as verification server performance will allow, typically at least 100,000 iterations.
2.4.4 — Verify that if bcrypt is used, the work factor SHOULD be as large as verification server performance will allow, typically at least 13.

2.4.5 — Verify that an additional iteration of a key derivation function is performed using a salt value secret and known only to the verifier. The secret salt value SHALL be stored separately from the hashed passwords (e.g., in a hardware security module).
